passage:
Volunteer coordinator's note, Saturday. Arohi.
Tenzin, our twenty-year-old intern, ran the welcome desk at the neighbourhood blood-donation camp, and I watched him closely. When old Pandit-ji arrived, Tenzin bent to touch his feet; Pandit-ji beamed. With Dr. Fatima he paused, saw her hand come forward, and shook it. For the two nuns from the convent he simply joined his palms and smiled, and they did the same. A college student got a high five. Afterwards I asked how he decided. He said, 'I just watched what their hands did first.' At the next camp I'll have him train the new volunteers.

qa.q: How did Tenzin greet Dr. Fatima?
qa.a: He saw her hand come forward and shook it.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's answer, 'I just watched what their hands did first', suggest about how he felt at the desk?
qa.a: It suggests he felt calm and attentive rather than anxious about rules, caring more about each person's comfort than a fixed custom.

qa.q: What could new volunteers learn from Tenzin?
qa.a: To pause and read each guest's cue, their hands, age and comfort, before choosing a bow, a handshake or folded hands.

qa.q: How might Dr. Fatima feel when Tenzin waits for her hand before shaking it?
qa.a: She would probably feel respected and at ease, since he followed her lead instead of assuming.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing between touching feet, a handshake, folded hands or a high five depending on each person, by reading their cue rather than following one fixed rule.

passage:
Sunday, late
Went to Mahima's sister's engagement. Nervous the whole way. At home it's easy: bend, touch feet, done. But Mahima's family is huge and mixed: her Nani is Bengali, her Dadi Punjabi, her Phuphu married into a Goan family. At the door her Dadi opened her arms wide, so I hugged her. Her Nani sat with folded hands, so I did a pranam and got a blessing. Her Goan uncle stuck out his hand: handshake. One very old man I bent toward, and he lifted me by the elbows, laughing, 'No need, no need!' I felt silly for a second, then warm. Next time: watch first, then greet.
Vandana

qa.q: Who stuck out a hand for a handshake?
What was Vandana feeling on the way to the engagement?
qa.a: Vandana felt nervous, unsure which greeting would suit each person in such a mixed family.

qa.q: What rule did Vandana end up with, and why is it wise?
qa.a: 'Watch first, then greet', because reading each person's cue is kinder than applying one fixed custom.

qa.q: How might the very old man have felt when Vandana bent toward his feet?
qa.a: He seemed touched but didn't want the formality, so he lifted Vandana up laughing, his own warm way of accepting the respect.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing between touching feet, folded hands, a hug or a handshake by reading each elder's cue in a mixed gathering.
